What if the deadliest thing on a sailing ship wasn't the cannons, but a missing piece of fruit?
On long voyages, sailors got weak. Their gums bled, and old wounds opened up again.
It was called scurvy, and by some estimates it killed more sailors than enemy guns.
In seventeen forty-seven, a ship's doctor named James Lind tried something new.
He split twelve sick sailors into pairs, and gave each pair a different cure.
Vinegar. Seawater. Cider. And two oranges and a lemon, every day.
The citrus pair got better so fast, one was back on his feet within days.
Even so, the Navy waited until seventeen ninety-five to hand out lemon juice.
Then, to save money, they swapped lemons for cheaper limes.
But limes have far less vitamin C, and scurvy crept back.
Nobody knew why until vitamin C was discovered, decades later.
Still, the name stuck. That's why British sailors are called limeys, after the fruit that almost worked.
